analysis.one_liner: Sets minimum federal standards for sports betting, letting states offer it only with strict consumer protections.
analysis.headline: Introduced with no cosponsors on September 16, 2024, and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it died without a hearing or a vote when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it unlawful to take a sports bet anywhere in the country unless a state applies for and receives federal approval to run a regulated program. States that opt in would have to follow a long list of federal standards: bettors must be 21 and verified, no credit-card deposits, a cap of 5 deposits a day, affordability checks above $1,000 in a day, bans on ads during daytime hours and on 'bonus' promotions, a national self-exclusion list for people who want to bar themselves from betting, and a share of operator revenue earmarked for gambling-addiction treatment and education. It would also fund a national survey of problem gambling, a Surgeon General's report, and a surveillance system for gambling addiction.
analysis.who_benefits: People who bet on sports and people at risk of gambling addiction — the bill's deposit limits, affordability checks, advertising bans, and national self-exclusion list are all aimed at curbing the way online sportsbooks chase heavy bettors. Families of problem gamblers would benefit from treatment and education funding, and professional and college sports would gain new tools to keep suspicious bets off their games.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Sports bettors and people at risk of gambling addiction

how_it_helps.text: Bans credit-card deposits, caps deposits at 5 per 24 hours, and requires an affordability check — verifying deposits against income or creditworthiness — before a bettor can put in more than $1,000 a day or $10,000 in 30 days.
Creates a national self-exclusion list, run with state regulators, so a person can bar themselves from sports betting in every participating state at once, not just one app at a time.

Restricts advertising: no ads from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m., none during live games, no 'bonus' or 'no sweat' offers, and bans using artificial intelligence to track individual bettors or target them with personalized promotions or products like microbets.

Requires operators to fund treatment for gambling disorder and education on responsible gaming, and funds an annual national survey on problem gambling, a Surgeon General's report on sports betting's public health effects, and a CDC-run gambling-addiction surveillance system that the gambling industry may not fund or direct.
Prohibits proposition bets on college and amateur sports, blocks wagers after a game has started, and lets sports leagues request restrictions on bets that could compromise a contest's integrity.

Bans withdrawing winnings as a condition of participating in operator publicity, prohibits withdrawal limits and dormancy fees, and requires operators to hold reserves covering patron balances and unpaid winnings.

analysis.who_pays: Online sports betting operators, which would face a federal prohibition with an 18-month runway, state-by-state licensing, heavy compliance and recordkeeping duties, advertising restrictions that cut off their main customer-acquisition channel, and limits on deposit methods and sizes that hit their highest-revenue bettors hardest. Broadcasters and sports media that carry sportsbook ads, and bettors who would face more friction placing large or frequent bets, would also bear costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Online sports betting operators and their advertisers

drawbacks.text: The federal prohibition plus state opt-in structure would override the patchwork of state laws already in place, forcing states that chose their own rules to reapply for federal approval and comply with one national template, and it would penalize unlawful bookmakers only with civil fines, not criminal charges.

Restricting legal betting so heavily — no daytime ads, deposit limits, affordability checks — could push some bettors toward offshore or illegal books that have none of the safeguards, and operators would likely pass compliance costs on to bettors in worse odds.

Recordkeeping rules would require operators to collect and verify names, addresses, birth dates, and Social Security or passport numbers for individual bets, expanding the amount of sensitive personal data tied to gambling activity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are the point of the bill and are substantive, not cosmetic: credit-card betting, algorithmic targeting of losing bettors, and bonus-lure advertising are the practices most tied to heavy gambling losses, and a national self-exclusion list fixes a real gap where self-banning app-by-app leaves a person one signup away from relapse. The trade-off is real too: it centralizes in Washington decisions states currently make themselves, its penalties are civil fines that may not deter offshore operators, and bettors who use sportsbooks responsibly would face more friction and likely worse odds. Whether the friction is worth it depends largely on how much weight you give the documented rise in gambling-related harm since states legalized online sports betting.

outcome.mechanism: Blumenthal introduced it in mid-September 2024 near the end of the two-year Congress, and it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the session ended.

narrative.text: Senator Blumenthal introduced the bill on September 16, 2024, with no cosponsors listed.

The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day; the full action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

The bill would have taken 18 months after enactment to impose its general prohibition on accepting sports wagers outside approved state programs, meaning any future version would start from scratch in a new Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online sports betting operators, which keep the current lighter state-by-state rules and avoid deposit caps, advertising bans, affordability checks, and mandatory addiction-treatment funding.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sports betting operators under the status quo

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill on September 16, 2024 and sent it to the Judiciary Committee.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 16, 2024 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors from either party and no votes on record, so the partisan shape of support or opposition was never tested.

industries.note: The bill does not ban legal sportsbooks — it lets them keep operating in states that opt in and even gives them a federal licensing framework — but it caps deposits, bans credit-card funding, restricts advertising, bars AI-targeted promotions, and earmarks revenue for addiction treatment, all of which cut into the high-frequency, high-loss betting that drives operator revenue. Its protections for bettors come directly out of practices the industry profits from.

Leagues get a statutory process to request restrictions on bets that could compromise game integrity, a ban on college and amateur proposition bets, and direct transmission of suspicious-transaction reports. This protects the fairness of the games fans watch.

The bill preserves tribal authority under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act and treats online bets as occurring on tribal lands when the server is on Indian lands under a tribal-state compact, opening a path for tribes to run online sportsbooks — but only within the same strict federal standards.

The ban on sportsbook advertising from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. and during live game broadcasts would eliminate a fast-growing ad revenue stream, including the in-game betting promotions that saturate broadcasts today. Their financial interest is in keeping the ads running, not in the bettor protections the ads are restricted for.
The ban on credit-card deposits removes a funding channel for betting; the industry's loss here is the point of the consumer protection.
